prompt:
A shop keeps its shopping cart in a reducer, as with React's `useReducer` or Redux. Write `cartReducer(state, action)`. It returns the next state. It must **never change** `state` or anything inside it (no `push`, no `item.qty += 1` on an existing object): build new objects and arrays instead.

The tests call `replayCart(actions)`, which is already written in the starter. It starts from the empty cart, runs each action through your reducer and returns the list of states after each action. Do not change it. If your reducer changes an old state in place, the earlier entries in that list change too and the test fails, in the same way a React component would miss an update.

**State**
```
{
  items: [ { id, name, price, qty } ],   // lines, in the order they were first added
  coupon: null  or  { code, percent },
  subtotal, discount, total               // integers, in cents
}
```
The empty cart is `{ items: [], coupon: null, subtotal: 0, discount: 0, total: 0 }`.

**Actions**
- `{ type: "add", item: { id, name, price } }`: if a line with this `id` is already in the cart, its `qty` goes up by 1 (keep its name and price). Otherwise add `{ id, name, price, qty: 1 }` at the end. `price` is an integer number of cents.
- `{ type: "setQty", id, qty }`: set that line's quantity (`qty` is an integer). If `qty` is 0 or less, remove the line.
- `{ type: "remove", id }`: remove that line.
- `{ type: "applyCoupon", code }`: the known codes are `SAVE10` (10 percent off) and `HALF` (50 percent off). Compare codes ignoring upper/lower case and ignoring spaces at either end. A known code sets `coupon` to `{ code, percent }`, with the code in capitals exactly as written here, and replaces any earlier coupon. An unknown code changes nothing.
- `{ type: "removeCoupon" }`: set `coupon` to `null`.
- `{ type: "clear" }`: back to the empty cart (no lines, no coupon).
- Nothing changes for any other `type`, or for `setQty` / `remove` with an `id` that is not in the cart (`setQty` never adds a line).

**Quantity limit**: a line's `qty` is never more than 10. `add` on a line that already has 10 changes nothing. `setQty` above 10 sets it to 10.

**Totals**, recalculated after every action:
- `subtotal` = the sum of `price * qty` over all lines.
- `discount` = `Math.floor(subtotal * percent / 100)` when there is a coupon, otherwise 0.
- `total` = `subtotal - discount`.

**Example**
```
replayCart([
  { type: "add", item: { id: "p1", name: "Mug", price: 1250 } },
  { type: "add", item: { id: "p2", name: "Tea", price: 499 } },
  { type: "applyCoupon", code: "save10" }
])
-> [
  { items: [{ id: "p1", name: "Mug", price: 1250, qty: 1 }],
    coupon: null, subtotal: 1250, discount: 0, total: 1250 },
  { items: [{ id: "p1", name: "Mug", price: 1250, qty: 1 }, { id: "p2", name: "Tea", price: 499, qty: 1 }],
    coupon: null, subtotal: 1749, discount: 0, total: 1749 },
  { items: [ ...the same two lines... ],
    coupon: { code: "SAVE10", percent: 10 }, subtotal: 1749, discount: 174, total: 1575 }
]
```
explanation: A pure reducer: every action builds a new items array and new line objects for the lines that change, and every new state goes through one helper that recalculates subtotal, discount (Math.floor) and total, so the totals cannot go stale. The history returned by replayCart exposes in-place mutation: if a line object is changed instead of copied, earlier snapshots change too. Hidden tests check: no actions, adding the same item twice (snapshots must keep the old qty), a coupon applied before items are added (discount must follow later changes), codes with spaces and mixed case, an unknown code keeping the current coupon, the 10 limit on add and on setQty, setQty to 0 and below, setQty/remove for a missing id, an unknown action type, clear, a second coupon replacing the first, the floor on the discount and a 40-action mixed run. The wrong solutions are the common reducer bugs: mutating the existing line on add, storing the discount only when the coupon is applied, not trimming the code, forgetting the limit on add, and letting an unknown code wipe the current coupon.

hidden_tests.name: same item added twice keeps old snapshots
coupon applied before items are added
code with spaces and mixed case
unknown code keeps the current coupon
setQty to 0 and below removes the line
missing id changes nothing and setQty never adds
second coupon replaces the first, then removed
snapshots after setQty and add on the same line

wrong.why: changes the existing line in place on add (existing.qty += 1) and only copies the array, so earlier states in the history change too
calculates the discount only when the coupon is applied, so the discount goes stale when items change afterwards
compares the coupon code ignoring case but does not trim the spaces around it
applies the 10 limit in setQty only, so add can push a line above 10
an unknown coupon code removes the coupon that was already applied

quality_focus: no mutation of the previous state
totals derived in one place so they cannot go stale
clear handling of each action and of no-op cases

prompt:
A search box calls the search API while the user types. To avoid one request per key press, the call is **debounced**. Write `firedSearches(keystrokes, delayMs)`, which simulates this and returns the searches that are actually sent. (There is no real timer: you work it out from the timestamps.)

**Input**
- `keystrokes`: an array of `{ t, value }`. `t` is the time in milliseconds (an integer) and `value` is the full text in the box after that key press. The array is sorted by `t`; two keystrokes can have the same `t` (for example a paste).
- `delayMs`: an integer, at least 1.

**Rules**
- Every keystroke at time `t` starts a new timer for `t + delayMs` and cancels the timer that was waiting before it.
- A keystroke cancels the waiting timer only if it comes **before** that timer's time. A keystroke at exactly `t + delayMs` is too late: the timer fires first.
- After the last keystroke nothing cancels its timer, so it fires.
- When a timer fires, the query is that keystroke's `value` with spaces removed from both ends. The search is **not** sent if:
  - the query has fewer than 2 characters, or
  - the query is exactly the same text (upper/lower case matters) as the last query that was **sent**. Queries that fired but were not sent do not count as sent.

**Output**
An array of `{ at, query }` for the searches that are sent, in time order. `at` is the time the timer fired (`t + delayMs`).

**Example**
```
firedSearches([
  { t: 0,    value: "r" },
  { t: 100,  value: "re" },
  { t: 200,  value: "rea" },
  { t: 900,  value: "reac" },
  { t: 1000, value: "react" }
], 300)
-> [ { at: 500, query: "rea" }, { at: 1300, query: "react" } ]
```
The keystrokes at 100, 200 and 1000 each cancel the timer before them. The timer from 200 fires at 500 because nothing arrives before 500.
explanation: A keystroke's timer fires unless the next keystroke arrives strictly before t + delayMs, so a single pass that looks at the next keystroke is enough. A fired query is trimmed, skipped if shorter than 2 characters, and skipped if it equals the last query actually sent. Hidden tests check: no keystrokes, a single keystroke, a single short keystroke, the exact boundary (a keystroke at t + delayMs does not cancel) and one millisecond before it, a query repeated after a short query in between, trailing spaces, spaces only, a paste with equal timestamps, case differences, steady typing just under the delay (only the last timer fires) and a 100+ keystroke session. The wrong solutions are realistic debounce bugs: <= at the boundary, remembering the last fired query instead of the last sent one, comparing untrimmed text, and not restarting the timer on each key (throttle-like behaviour).

hidden_tests.name: keystroke exactly at the fire time does not cancel
same query after a short one is not sent again
trailing spaces are the same query
steady typing just under the delay

wrong.why: a keystroke at exactly t + delayMs cancels the timer (<= instead of <)
compares with the last query that fired, even when it was not sent because it was too short
compares the untrimmed value with the last sent one, so "ab " is sent again after "ab"
starts the timer on the first key of a burst and does not restart it on later keys

quality_focus: timer boundary handled exactly
clear separation of "fired" and "sent"
single pass, no simulated clock ticking

prompt:
A product list page keeps its filters in the URL, so users can share and bookmark a search. Write `buildQueryString(filters)`, which turns the filters object into the query string part of the URL.

**Input**
`filters` is an object. Each value is a string, a number, `true`, `false`, `null`, or an array whose items are strings, numbers or `null`.

**Rules**
- Keys are written in ascending plain character order (the order `<` gives for strings, so capital letters come before lower-case ones). The same filters must always give the same string.
- A key is left out when its value is `null`, `false`, a string that is empty after trimming, or an array with no items left after the array rules below.
- `true` is written as `true`. Numbers are written with `String(n)`. **`0` is a real value** and is kept.
- Strings are trimmed (spaces removed from both ends).
- An array gives one `key=value` pair per item, in the array's order. Items that are `null` or empty after trimming are skipped. Items are trimmed like strings. If the same text appears more than once, write it only the first time (`42` and `"42"` count as the same text).
- Encode every key and every value with `encodeURIComponent`.
- Join the pairs with `&` and put `?` in front. If there are no pairs at all, return the empty string `""`.

**Example**
```
buildQueryString({ q: " red shoes ", size: [42, 43], inStock: true, brand: "", page: 1, sort: null })
-> "?inStock=true&page=1&q=red%20shoes&size=42&size=43"
```
explanation: Sort the keys, turn each value into a list of texts (null, false and blank strings give nothing, true gives "true", numbers use String, strings and array items are trimmed, repeated texts are dropped), then encode key and value with encodeURIComponent. Hidden tests check: an empty object, everything skipped, 0 as a value and as an array item, characters that must be encoded (&, =, %, #, /, +), false skipped, key order with capitals and digits, repeated array items, null and blank items inside arrays, negative and decimal numbers, non-ASCII text, keys that need encoding, whitespace-only strings and a 30-key object. The wrong solutions are the usual ones: a truthiness check that drops 0, encodeURI on the whole string (leaves & = + # / unencoded), no de-duplication, writing false as "false", and arrays whose items are not trimmed or filtered.

hidden_tests.name: key order with capitals and digits

wrong.why: skips values with a truthiness check, so 0 (as a value or an array item) disappears
uses encodeURI on the whole string, which leaves & = + # / unencoded inside values
writes repeated array items more than once
writes false as "false" instead of leaving the key out
array items are not trimmed and null or blank items are not skipped

quality_focus: 0 and false handled on purpose, not by truthiness
correct URL encoding
small helpers with clear names

prompt:
A comment list shows when each comment was posted ("5 minutes ago", "yesterday"). Write `relativeTime(nowMs, thenMs)`, which returns that label.

**Input**
Two integers: milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC (what `Date.now()` returns). `nowMs` is the current time and `thenMs` is when the comment was posted. Work in **UTC** only (use `getUTC...` methods or plain arithmetic).

**Rules**, with `diff = nowMs - thenMs`, checked in this order:
1. `diff` below 60,000 ms (one minute): `"just now"`. This includes a `thenMs` later than `nowMs` (a device clock that is slightly wrong).
2. `diff` below one hour: `"1 minute ago"` or `"N minutes ago"`, where N is the number of **whole** minutes (round down).
3. `diff` below 24 hours: `"1 hour ago"` or `"N hours ago"`, whole hours, rounded down.
4. Otherwise count **calendar days** in UTC: `days` = the UTC date of `nowMs` minus the UTC date of `thenMs`, in days (for example, from 3 October 23:00 to 5 October 01:00 is 2 days). Then:
   - `days` is 1: `"yesterday"`
   - `days` is 2 to 6: `"N days ago"`
   - otherwise, if `thenMs` is in the same UTC year as `nowMs`: month and day, like `"Mar 5"`
   - otherwise: month, day and year, like `"Dec 31, 2025"`

Month names: `Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec`. The day has no leading zero.

**Example**
```
const now = 1791115200000;              // 2026-10-04 12:00:00 UTC
relativeTime(now, now - 30000)          -> "just now"
relativeTime(now, now - 5 * 60000)      -> "5 minutes ago"
relativeTime(now, now - 5 * 3600000)    -> "5 hours ago"
relativeTime(now, 1791014400000)        -> "yesterday"      // 2026-10-03 08:00 UTC, 28 hours earlier
relativeTime(now, 1790848800000)        -> "3 days ago"     // 2026-10-01 10:00 UTC
relativeTime(now, 1772704800000)        -> "Mar 5"          // 2026-03-05 10:00 UTC
relativeTime(now, 1767225540000)        -> "Dec 31, 2025"   // 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC
```
explanation: Compare the elapsed time against one minute, one hour and one day with strict <, rounding down; after 24 hours switch to calendar days in UTC (floor(ms / DAY) gives the UTC day number), then "yesterday", "N days ago", or a date with the year only when it differs from now's UTC year. Hidden tests check: the exact minute, hour and day boundaries, future and equal timestamps, hours across midnight, two calendar days apart but only 25.5 hours, 6 versus 7 calendar days, a same-year date, a previous-year date less than a year ago, a leap day, round-down versus round, singular units and 40 generated cases. The wrong solutions are: no singular form, counting elapsed 24-hour blocks instead of calendar days, Math.round instead of Math.floor, deciding the year by "less than 365 days ago", and <= at the boundaries.

hidden_tests.name: previous year, less than a year ago

wrong.why: always uses the plural ("1 minutes ago", "1 hours ago")
counts elapsed 24-hour periods instead of calendar days, so 26 hours across two midnights is "yesterday"
rounds minutes and hours to the nearest instead of down (90 seconds becomes "2 minutes ago")
hides the year when the date is less than 365 days ago, instead of comparing calendar years
uses <= at the boundaries, so exactly 60 seconds is still "just now"

quality_focus: named time constants instead of magic numbers
boundaries and calendar days handled exactly
one small helper for the plural form

prompt:
A data table needs page links like `‹ 1 ... 4 5 6 ... 20 ›`. Write `paginationItems(current, total, siblings)`, which works out what to show. (Rendering is not part of the task.)

**Input** (all integers)
- `current`: the page the URL asks for. It can be outside the real range (an old link such as `?page=99`, or `0`).
- `total`: the number of pages, 0 or more.
- `siblings`: how many pages to show on each side of the current page, 0 or more.

**Output**
`{ current, prev, next, items }`
- `current`: the page actually shown: the input clamped into the range 1 to `total`.
- `prev`: `current - 1`, or `null` on the first page. `next`: `current + 1`, or `null` on the last page.
- `items`: page numbers (numbers) and gaps (the string `"..."`), from left to right.
- When `total` is 0: `{ current: null, prev: null, next: null, items: [] }`.

**Rules for `items`** (after clamping `current`)
- If `total` ≤ `2 * siblings + 5`: every page from 1 to `total`.
- Otherwise the list always has exactly `2 * siblings + 5` entries:
  - **Near the start**, when `current` ≤ `siblings + 3`: pages 1 to `2 * siblings + 3`, then `"..."`, then `total`.
  - **Near the end**, when `current` ≥ `total - siblings - 2`: `1`, `"..."`, then the last `2 * siblings + 3` pages.
  - **Otherwise**: `1`, `"..."`, pages `current - siblings` to `current + siblings`, `"..."`, `total`.

**Example**
```
paginationItems(5, 20, 1) -> { current: 5, prev: 4, next: 6, items: [1, "...", 4, 5, 6, "...", 20] }
paginationItems(2, 20, 1) -> { current: 2, prev: 1, next: 3, items: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, "...", 20] }
paginationItems(3, 6, 1)  -> { current: 3, prev: 2, next: 4, items: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] }
```
explanation: Handle total 0 first, clamp current into 1..total, derive prev/next from the clamped page, then pick one of four layouts: all pages, near the start, near the end, or the middle window. Hidden tests check: no pages, one page, current above total and below 1, both thresholds exactly and one past them, total equal to and one above 2*siblings+5, siblings 0 and 2, the last page, a very large total, and every page of a 12-page table. The wrong solutions are: no clamping, thresholds off by one (a gap that hides just one page), < instead of <= for the show-everything case, no special case for 0 pages, and a plain window that does not keep the length constant near the edges.

hidden_tests.name: total exactly the number of slots, and one more

wrong.why: does not clamp current, so ?page=99 gives next: 100 and a wrong window
near-start and near-end thresholds are off by one, so a gap can hide a single page
uses < instead of <= for the "show every page" case, so 7 pages with siblings 1 get a gap
no special case for 0 pages: returns current 1 instead of nulls
shows a plain window around current without filling up to a constant length near the edges

quality_focus: clamp first, then derive everything from the clamped page
readable layout branches with named values
edge cases (0 or 1 page)

prompt:
A data table lets users sort by several columns (click "Team", then shift-click "Score"). Write `sortRows(rows, sortBy)`, which returns the ids of the rows in the order the table should show them.

**Input**
- `rows`: an array of objects. Each has a unique string `id` plus other fields. In any one column the values are either all numbers or all strings, except that some values can be **missing**: `null`, `""` (empty string), or the key is not there at all.
- `sortBy`: an array of `{ key, dir }`, where `dir` is `"asc"` or `"desc"`. The first entry is the main sort; each later entry only decides between rows that are equal on all entries before it.

**Rules**
- Numbers are compared as numbers.
- Strings are compared **ignoring upper/lower case**: compare the lower-case versions with `<` (do not use `localeCompare`). Strings that are equal ignoring case count as equal.
- `"desc"` reverses the order of real values.
- **Missing values always go last**, in both directions. Two missing values count as equal.
- Rows that are equal on every `sortBy` entry keep their original order (a stable sort). With an empty `sortBy`, the original order is returned.
- Do not change `rows`.

**Output**
An array of the row `id`s in sorted order.

**Example**
```
const rows = [
  { id: "a", name: "Zoe",  team: "Web", score: 90 },
  { id: "b", name: "adam", team: "web", score: 72 },
  { id: "c", name: "Bea",  team: "API", score: 75 },
  { id: "d", name: "Cal",  team: "Web", score: 90 },
  { id: "e", name: "Dan",  team: null,  score: 60 }
];
sortRows(rows, [{ key: "team", dir: "asc" }, { key: "score", dir: "desc" }])
-> ["c", "a", "d", "b", "e"]
```
"API" comes first. "Web" and "web" are equal, so score decides (a and d tie on 90 and keep their order). e has no team, so it is last.
explanation: One comparator walks the sortBy entries in order: missing values (null, undefined, "") go last before the direction is applied, strings compare lower-cased with <, the first non-zero result decides (negated for desc), and the original index breaks full ties. Hidden tests check: no rows, an empty sortBy, missing values in a desc column, null/""/absent keys together in both directions, case-insensitive ties falling through to the next key, three keys with mixed directions, many full ties (stability), 9 versus 10 as numbers, negative and decimal numbers, a column where every value is missing, one row and 1,000 generated rows. The wrong solutions are common comparator bugs: applying desc to missing values too (they jump to the top), comparing strings case-sensitively, one sort call per column in the chosen order (the last column wins), a comparator that never returns 0, comparing numbers as strings, and treating "" as a real value.

hidden_tests.name: missing values last in a desc column
null, empty string and absent key, both directions
case-insensitive ties fall through to the next key
full ties keep their original order
a column where every value is missing

wrong.why: applies the desc direction to missing values too, so they move to the top in desc columns
compares strings case-sensitively, so "Web" and "web" are not equal and capitals sort first
calls sort once per column in the order given, so the last column becomes the main sort
comparator never returns 0 for full ties (returns -1), so equal rows lose their original order
compares every value as a string, so 10 sorts before 9
treats the empty string as a real value instead of missing

quality_focus: one comparator with a clear order of checks
missing values handled before the direction is applied
stable result without mutating the input

prompt:
A signup form shows an error under each field. Write `validateSignup(form)`, which returns those errors so the same rules can run on every change and before submit.

**Input**
`form` is an object with the fields below. Any field can be missing; a missing text field counts as the empty string.

**Rules.** Check each field's rules in the order listed and report only the **first** rule that fails for that field.

`username`: spaces at both ends are removed first.
1. Empty: `"Username is required"`
2. Shorter than 3 or longer than 20 characters: `"Username must be 3 to 20 characters"`
3. Has any character other than English letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9) or `_`: `"Username can only contain letters, numbers and _"`

`email`: spaces at both ends are removed first.
1. Empty: `"Email is required"`
2. Not valid: `"Enter a valid email address"`. Valid means all of these: no spaces inside it; exactly one `@`; at least one character before the `@`; and the part after the `@` splits on `.` into at least two pieces, none of them empty (`a@b.co` is valid; `a@b`, `a@b.`, `a@.b` and `a@b..co` are not).

`password`: **not** trimmed (spaces count as characters).
1. Empty: `"Password is required"`
2. Shorter than 8 characters: `"Password must be at least 8 characters"`
3. Does not contain at least one English letter **and** at least one digit: `"Password must contain a letter and a number"`

`confirmPassword`: checked **only when `password` has no error**. If it is not exactly the same as `password`: `"Passwords do not match"`

`age`: optional. `null`, missing, or a string that is empty after trimming means "not given" and is fine. Otherwise it must be either a number that is a whole number, or a string that, after trimming, is only digits. Its value must be from 13 to 120 (both included). If any of this fails: `"Age must be a whole number from 13 to 120"`

`acceptTerms`: must be exactly `true` (not `"true"`, not `1`). Otherwise: `"You must accept the terms"`

**Output**
An object with one key per field that has an error, and its message. A valid form gives `{}`.

**Example**
```
validateSignup({ username: "jo", email: "jo@site", password: "secret", confirmPassword: "secret",
                 age: "17", acceptTerms: false })
-> {
  username: "Username must be 3 to 20 characters",
  email: "Enter a valid email address",
  password: "Password must be at least 8 characters",
  acceptTerms: "You must accept the terms"
}
```
explanation: One small function per field that returns the first failing message or null, run in order, plus the cross-field rule (confirm only when the password itself is fine). Hidden tests check: an empty form, whitespace-only username and email, the first-failing-rule order for the username, length limits 3 and 20, seven email shapes, a password of spaces (not trimmed), letters-only and digits-only passwords, the confirm rule with a valid and an invalid password, case-sensitive confirm, eleven age values (13, 120, 12, 121, "  45 ", "45.0", 30.5, "abc", null, "", "1e2"), and acceptTerms "true" and 1. The wrong solutions: not trimming the username, reporting the last failing rule instead of the first, checking confirm even when the password already has an error, parsing age with Number() (accepts "45.0" and "1e2"), a truthy check on acceptTerms, and an email check that only looks for a dot after the @.

prompt:
A side menu is a tree that users can expand and collapse. To render it as a flat, accessible list (`role="treeitem"` with `aria-level`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-posinset`, `aria-setsize`), write `visibleRows(tree, collapsedIds)`, which returns the rows to show.

**Input**
- `tree`: an array of top-level nodes. A node is `{ id, label, children, hidden }`. `children` is an array of nodes and may be missing or empty. `hidden` may be missing (meaning `false`).
- `collapsedIds`: an array of node ids the user has collapsed. Ids that are not in the tree are ignored.

**Rules**
- A node with `hidden: true` is not shown, and nothing inside it is shown either. Hidden nodes do not count anywhere below (not in `hasChildren`, `posInSet` or `setSize`).
- `hasChildren`: the node has at least one child that is not hidden.
- `expanded`: `true` when `hasChildren` is true and the node's id is **not** in `collapsedIds`; otherwise `false` (a node with no children to show is never expanded).
- The children of a node are shown only when it is `expanded`. So a collapsed node hides all of its descendants, even ones that are not collapsed themselves.
- Order: depth-first. A node comes right before its shown children (in their array order), and all of them come before the node's next sibling.

**Output**
An array of rows `{ id, depth, path, hasChildren, expanded, posInSet, setSize }`:
- `depth`: 0 for top-level nodes, 1 for their children, and so on.
- `path`: the labels from the top-level node down to this node, joined with `" / "`.
- `posInSet`: the node's position (starting at 1) among its siblings that are not hidden. `setSize`: how many siblings that are not hidden there are, including the node.

**Example**
```
const tree = [
  { id: "home", label: "Home" },
  { id: "settings", label: "Settings", children: [
    { id: "account", label: "Account", children: [{ id: "password", label: "Password" }] },
    { id: "privacy", label: "Privacy", children: [{ id: "cookies", label: "Cookies" }] }
  ] },
  { id: "help", label: "Help", children: [] }
];
visibleRows(tree, ["privacy"])
-> [
  { id: "home",     depth: 0, path: "Home",                          hasChildren: false, expanded: false, posInSet: 1, setSize: 3 },
```

prompt:
When a keyed list re-renders (`key={item.id}` in React), the framework compares the old and new order of ids to decide which DOM nodes to create, delete and move. Write `diffKeyedList(oldIds, newIds)`, which does this comparison.

**Input**
Two arrays of non-empty strings: the ids before and after the update. Lists can hold thousands of ids, so avoid searching an array inside a loop (use a `Map` or `Set`).

**Rules**
1. **Duplicates.** Keys must be unique. If `oldIds` has an id twice, return `{ error: "duplicate id: <id>" }` for the **first position where an id appears for the second time**, reading left to right. Check `oldIds` first; only if it has no duplicate, check `newIds` the same way. Do nothing else in that case.
2. `added`: ids in `newIds` that are not in `oldIds`, in `newIds` order.
3. `removed`: ids in `oldIds` that are not in `newIds`, in `oldIds` order.
4. `moved` uses the same rule as React. Walk `newIds` from left to right and remember `lastPlaced`, the highest old index (position in `oldIds`) of an id that stayed in place so far; it starts at -1. For each id that is in **both** lists, with old index `i`:
   - if `i < lastPlaced`, the id is **moved**: add it to `moved` (so `moved` is in `newIds` order);
   - otherwise it stays in place and `lastPlaced` becomes `i`.
   Ids that are only in `newIds` do not change `lastPlaced`.

**Output**
`{ added, removed, moved }` (three arrays, possibly empty), or `{ error }` as described in rule 1.

**Example**
```
diffKeyedList(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"], ["b", "x", "a", "d", "c"])
-> { added: ["x"], removed: ["e"], moved: ["a", "c"] }
```
Walking the new list: `b` (old index 1) stays, so `lastPlaced` = 1. `x` is new. `a` (0) is below 1, so it moved. `d` (3) stays, `lastPlaced` = 3. `c` (2) is below 3, so it moved.
```
diffKeyedList(["a", "b", "a", "b"], ["a"])
-> { error: "duplicate id: a" }
```
explanation: Check duplicates with a Set (old list first, stopping at the first second occurrence), index the old list in a Map, then make one pass over the new list: unknown ids are added, ids whose old index is below lastPlaced are moved, others update lastPlaced. Removed ids come from one filter over the old list with a Set of new ids. Hidden tests check: two empty lists, everything new, everything removed, an unchanged list, the last item moved to the front (React's worst case: everything after it is moved), the first item moved to the end, a full reversal (moved must be in new order), duplicates in the new list only, duplicates in both lists (old wins), the first second occurrence versus the first id that has a copy, a mix of adds/removes/moves and a 3,000-id list. The wrong solutions: updating lastPlaced even for moved items, marking every id whose position changed, listing moved ids in old order, checking the new list for duplicates first, and reporting the first id that has a copy instead of the first repeat.

first item moved to the end
duplicate only in the new list
duplicates in both lists, old list first
first repeat, not first id with a copy

wrong.why: updates lastPlaced for moved ids too, so after one move the following ids look in place
marks every kept id whose position changed as moved, instead of following the lastPlaced rule
returns moved ids in their old order instead of the new order
checks newIds for duplicates before oldIds
reports the first id that has any copy, not the first position where an id repeats

the lastPlaced rule written clearly

prompt:
A small client-side router decides which page to show for the current URL. Write `matchRoute(routes, url)`.

**Input**
- `routes`: an array of route patterns such as `"/users/:id/posts/:postId"`.
- `url`: the path the browser is on. It can include a query string (`?tab=1`) and/or a hash (`#top`).

**Rules**
1. Cut `url` at the first `?` or `#`, whichever comes first, and use only the part before it.
2. Split the path and each pattern on `/` into **segments**, dropping empty ones. So `"/users/"`, `"/users"` and `"//users"` are all `["users"]`, and `"/"` and `""` are `[]`.
3. Kinds of pattern segment:
   - **Static text** (`users`): matches a URL segment equal to it, **ignoring upper/lower case**. Compare with the URL segment as it is (not decoded).
   - **`:name`**: matches any one segment. `params[name]` is that segment decoded with `decodeURIComponent`. If decoding throws (a broken `%` sequence), this route does not match and you try the next route.
   - **`:name?`** (optional): appears only at the end of a pattern (one or more of them). It works like `:name` when the URL has a segment there. When the URL has run out of segments, it matches nothing and `name` is **left out** of `params`.
   - **`*`**: appears only as the last segment of a pattern. It matches all remaining segments, **zero or more**. `params["*"]` is those segments joined with `/`, **not decoded** (`""` when there are none).
4. A route matches only when every URL segment is used (unless the pattern ends with `*`), and every segment of the pattern that is not optional or `*` has a URL segment.
5. The **first** route in `routes` that matches wins.

**Output**
`{ route, params }`, where `route` is the pattern string exactly as given and `params` is an object (`{}` when there are none). Return `null` if no route matches.

**Example**
```
const routes = ["/", "/users", "/users/new", "/users/:id", "/users/:id/posts/:postId", "/files/*", "/search/:term?"];

matchRoute(routes, "/users/42/posts/7?tab=comments") -> { route: "/users/:id/posts/:postId", params: { id: "42", postId: "7" } }
matchRoute(routes, "/users/new/")                    -> { route: "/users/new", params: {} }
matchRoute(routes, "/users/42/edit")                 -> null
matchRoute(routes, "/files/docs/My%20CV.pdf")        -> { route: "/files/*", params: { "*": "docs/My%20CV.pdf" } }
matchRoute(routes, "/search")                        -> { route: "/search/:term?", params: {} }
```
explanation: Strip everything from the first ? or #, split into non-empty segments, then try each pattern in order: static pieces compare lower-cased, :name decodes inside try/catch (a broken escape makes only this route fail), optional params are skipped when the URL has run out, * takes the raw rest (possibly empty), and leftover URL segments mean no match. Hidden tests check: the root path in several spellings, a hash, a hash before a query, case-insensitive statics with case-preserving params, first-match order when a param route is listed before a static one, repeated and trailing slashes, decoding (UTF-8 and an encoded slash), a broken escape falling through to the next route, a splat with zero segments, one and two optional params, no routes, too few and too many segments, and 40 URLs against a 26-route table. The wrong solutions: keeping the hash, case-sensitive statics, letting decodeURIComponent throw, a splat that needs at least one segment, handling only one leading/trailing slash, and setting missing optional params to null.

hidden_tests.name: static text ignores case, params keep it
broken escape falls through to the next route

wrong.why: cuts the URL at ? but not at #, so a hash ends up in the last segment
compares static segments case-sensitively
does not catch decodeURIComponent errors, so a broken % sequence throws instead of trying the next route
* needs at least one segment, so "/files" does not match "/files/*"
removes only one leading and one trailing slash instead of dropping every empty segment
sets a missing optional param to null instead of leaving it out

quality_focus: URL cleaning separated from pattern matching
decode errors handled without crashing
clear handling of each segment kind

prompt:
A long list is virtualised: only the rows near the viewport are rendered, inside a spacer as tall as the whole list. Write `visibleRange(input)`, which works out which rows to render for the current scroll position.

**Input**
`{ scrollTop, viewportHeight, itemCount, itemHeight, overscan }`
- `scrollTop`: the scroll position in pixels. It can be **negative** or **past the end** (the bounce effect on touch screens), and it can have a fractional part.
- `viewportHeight`: the visible height in pixels, at least 1.
- `itemCount`: the number of rows, 0 or more.
- `itemHeight`: either one number (every row has this height), or an array of `itemCount` heights. Heights are whole numbers, at least 1.
- `overscan`: extra rows to render above and below the visible ones (0 or more).

**Rules**
1. Row `i` covers the pixels from `top(i)` up to, **but not including**, `top(i) + height(i)`. Row 0 starts at 0, and each row starts where the one before it ends. `totalHeight` is the sum of all heights.
2. First clamp `scrollTop` into the range from 0 to `max(0, totalHeight - viewportHeight)`.
3. The viewport covers the pixels from `scrollTop` up to, but not including, `scrollTop + viewportHeight`. A row is **visible** if it shares at least part of a pixel range with the viewport: `top(i) < scrollTop + viewportHeight` and `top(i) + height(i) > scrollTop`. A row that ends exactly at `scrollTop`, or starts exactly at `scrollTop + viewportHeight`, is not visible.
4. `start` = (first visible row) − `overscan`, but not below 0. `end` = (last visible row) + `overscan`, but not above `itemCount - 1`.
5. `offsetTop` = `top(start)`: where the first rendered row is placed.
6. If `itemCount` is 0, return `{ start: 0, end: -1, offsetTop: 0, totalHeight: 0 }`.

**Size.** When `itemHeight` is a number, `itemCount` can be as large as 200,000,000 (a log viewer), so in that case do not loop over the rows or build an array with one entry per row. When it is an array, it has at most 50,000 entries.

**Output**
`{ start, end, offsetTop, totalHeight }` (`end` is included in the rows to render).

**Example**
```
visibleRange({ scrollTop: 120, viewportHeight: 100, itemCount: 1000, itemHeight: 50, overscan: 2 })
-> { start: 0, end: 6, offsetTop: 0, totalHeight: 50000 }
// rows 2, 3 and 4 are visible (pixels 120 to 219); 2 rows of overscan on each side

visibleRange({ scrollTop: 105, viewportHeight: 60, itemCount: 6, itemHeight: [30, 50, 20, 40, 60, 10], overscan: 1 })
-> { start: 2, end: 5, offsetTop: 80, totalHeight: 210 }
// rows start at 0, 30, 80, 100, 140, 200; rows 3 and 4 are visible (pixels 105 to 164)
```
explanation: Clamp scrollTop first. For a fixed height the visible rows are pure arithmetic: first = floor(top / h), last = ceil((top + viewport) / h) - 1, capped at itemCount - 1, so a 200-million-row list is O(1). For an array, build prefix sums once and binary-search the first row ending after top and the last row starting before the bottom edge (a linear scan also passes for 50,000 rows). Then apply overscan with clamping and read offsetTop from the start row. Hidden tests check: no rows, rows aligned exactly with both viewport edges (fixed and variable heights), negative and past-the-end scrollTop, content shorter than the viewport, overscan at the bottom, overscan 0, a fractional scrollTop, a row taller than the viewport, a single row, a 200,000,000-row fixed list, and a 5,000-row variable list at three positions. The wrong solutions: expanding a fixed height into an array and scanning it (runs out of memory or time), treating the bottom edge as inclusive, treating a row ending exactly at scrollTop as visible, not clamping scrollTop, and not capping end at itemCount - 1.

hidden_tests.name: rows aligned with both edges, fixed height
rows aligned with both edges, variable heights

wrong.why: expands a fixed height into one array entry per row and scans every row, which fails on a 200,000,000-row list
treats the bottom edge as inclusive, so a row starting exactly at scrollTop + viewportHeight counts as visible
treats a row that ends exactly at scrollTop as visible
does not clamp scrollTop, so a negative or past-the-end scroll position gives the wrong rows
does not cap end at itemCount - 1 when adding overscan

prompt:
A note-taking app needs undo and redo for a single text field, grouped the way users expect: a burst of typing is undone in one step, not one letter at a time. Write `editor(command)`. It receives one command per call and returns the field's state after that command.

**State.** Keep the editor's state at module level (outside the function). Each test starts a fresh program with an empty field (`text` is `""`, `cursor` is 0, no history) and then sends its commands in order.

**Commands**
- `{ op: "type", text, time }`: insert `text` (never empty) at the cursor; the cursor moves to just after the inserted text.
- `{ op: "backspace", time }`: delete the one character before the cursor and move the cursor back by one. If the cursor is at 0, nothing changes and no history step is made.
- `{ op: "move", to }`: put the cursor at `to`, clamped into the range 0 to `text.length`. This is not a history step.
- `{ op: "undo" }`: if there is a step to undo, put `text` **and** `cursor` back to what they were before that step, and make the step available to redo. Otherwise nothing changes.
- `{ op: "redo" }`: if there is a step to redo, put `text` and `cursor` back to what they were right after that step, and make it available to undo again. Otherwise nothing changes.

`time` is in milliseconds and never goes down from one command to the next.

**History steps**
- Every `type`, and every `backspace` that deletes a character, is one history step, **except** that it is merged into the step before it (making that step bigger) when **both** are true:
  - the command just before it (whatever it was, even one that changed nothing) has the **same `op`**, and
  - it comes **less than 1000 ms** after that command (`time - previousTime < 1000`).
  So a `move`, `undo`, `redo` or a different op in between always starts a new step.
- A new step (not a merge) **clears everything that could be redone**.
- At most **50 steps** can be undone. When a 51st step is added, the oldest one is forgotten.

**Output** of every call: `{ text, cursor, canUndo, canRedo }`, where `canUndo` / `canRedo` say whether an undo / redo would do anything right now.

**Example** (one test, in order)
```
editor({ op: "type", text: "Hello", time: 0 })     -> { text: "Hello",        cursor: 5,  canUndo: true,  canRedo: false }
editor({ op: "type", text: " world", time: 400 })  -> { text: "Hello world",  cursor: 11, canUndo: true,  canRedo: false }  // merged
editor({ op: "move", to: 5 })                      -> { text: "Hello world",  cursor: 5,  canUndo: true,  canRedo: false }
editor({ op: "type", text: ",", time: 600 })       -> { text: "Hello, world", cursor: 6,  canUndo: true,  canRedo: false }  // new step: a move came between
editor({ op: "undo" })                             -> { text: "Hello world",  cursor: 5,  canUndo: true,  canRedo: true }
editor({ op: "undo" })                             -> { text: "",             cursor: 0,  canUndo: false, canRedo: true }
editor({ op: "redo" })                             -> { text: "Hello world",  cursor: 11, canUndo: true,  canRedo: true }
```
explanation: Two stacks of steps, each step storing the text and cursor before and after it. An edit merges into the top step only when the command just before it had the same op and came less than 1000 ms earlier; otherwise it pushes a new step, drops the oldest beyond 50 and clears the redo stack. Undo restores "before" (text and cursor) and moves the step to the redo stack; redo restores "after" and moves it back. Every command, even a no-op, becomes "the previous command". Hidden tests check: typing in the middle of the text, backspace bursts and the 1000 ms boundary (999 merges, 1000 does not), a new edit clearing redo, merging broken by undo, by a different op and by a move, backspace at position 0 (no step), undo/redo on an empty history, move clamping, redo restoring a mid-text cursor, the 50-step limit with 60 steps, and an 80-command mixed session. The wrong solutions: not clearing redo on a new step, grouping by time only (broken only by move), <= at the 1000 ms boundary, redo putting the cursor at the end of the text, no 50-step limit, recording a step for a backspace that deletes nothing, and not clamping move.
